definition: Treating network weights as distributions rather than point estimates, so predictions come with principled uncertainty.
details: Treating network weights as distributions rather than point estimates, so predictions come with principled uncertainty. Exact posteriors are intractable at scale, so the practice lives in approximations: variational methods, SWAG, Laplace, and the pragmatic stand-ins below.

explainer.lead: Bayesian deep learning treats a neural network’s weights as a range of plausible values rather than one fixed answer. This lets predictions reflect uncertainty, which is useful when knowing how sure a model is matters as much as the prediction itself.

tiers.eli5: Imagine guessing what is in a blurry photo. Instead of trusting just one guess, you consider several reasonable ways of looking at it and see how much they agree. Bayesian deep learning does something similar with a network’s settings, so it can say both what it predicts and how uncertain that prediction is.
tiers.practitioner: Instead of optimizing only point-estimate weights, approximate the weight posterior and integrate predictions over it. Exact inference is intractable at scale, so common practical choices include variational methods, SWAG, and Laplace approximations. The main pitfalls are approximation error and treating the resulting uncertainty as automatically reliable or well calibrated.
tiers.paperLevel: Given data D, the predictive distribution is p(y*|x*,D) = integral p(y*|x*,w) p(w|D) dw, where p(w|D) is the posterior over network weights. Because exact posterior computation is intractable at scale, variational inference, SWAG, and Laplace approximations provide practical substitutes. These approximations can differ from the true posterior, so principled uncertainty does not imply exact or calibrated uncertainty.

explainer.example: For a blurry animal photo, a Bayesian image classifier combines predictions from many plausible weight settings. If those settings mostly favour cat but some favour dog, the output might be 70% cat and 30% dog, exposing uncertainty that a single confident cat prediction would hide.
explainer.intuition: Many different weight settings may explain the training data reasonably well. Keeping that range of possibilities, instead of selecting only one setting, allows their disagreement to appear as uncertainty in predictions.
howItWorks: Represent network weights with probability distributions rather than single point estimates.
Use the observed data to update beliefs about which weight values are plausible, forming a posterior distribution.
Approximate this posterior with methods such as variational inference, SWAG, or Laplace when exact computation is intractable.
Combine predictions across plausible weights to obtain a predictive distribution rather than only a single output.
explainer.whyItMatters: It gives neural networks a principled way to express uncertainty alongside predictions. That can make ambiguous or unfamiliar inputs visible instead of hiding them behind one point estimate.
misconceptions: It does not make exact Bayesian inference practical for large networks; scalable implementations rely on approximations.
A predictive distribution is not automatically accurate or well calibrated just because it was produced by a Bayesian method.
SWAG and Laplace approximations are practical ways to approximate weight uncertainty, not exact posterior computations.
